summary: This informational document describes an architecture based on a Path Computation Element (PCE) for MPLS and GMPLS networks. Computing constrained paths across large, multi-domain, multi-region or multi-layer networks is hard, so special computation components may cooperate. It describes building blocks rather than every component.

plainLanguage.summary: Planning a trip across many countries is hard for one traveler. A trip planner who knows all the maps can work out the route for you.

subtitle: A blueprint for handing constrained path computation in MPLS and GMPLS networks to dedicated, cooperating Path Computation Elements.

tldr.problem: Computing constrained paths across large, multi-domain, multi-region or multi-layer networks is complex, and the router at the head of a path often cannot see the whole network.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a Path Computation Element (PCE), an entity that computes a path from a network graph and constraints, and a Path Computation Client (PCC) that asks it. PCEs can sit inside routers or on separate servers, and several can cooperate.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational architecture, not a protocol. It lists building blocks and the areas that still need standardization, such as PCC-PCE communication and PCE discovery.

today: RFC 4655 is an Informational RFC published in August 2006, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It describes building blocks and leaves detailed protocols, discovery and MIB work to other documents.

sections.title: Introduction and Definitions
sections.content:
Constraint-based path computation is a basic building block of traffic engineering in MPLS and GMPLS networks. In large networks split into several domains (for example IGP areas or Autonomous Systems), that computation is complex and may need special components that cooperate across domains.

A Path Computation Element (PCE) is an entity that computes a network path or route based on a network graph and applies computational constraints. It can live inside a network node or on an out-of-network server. A PCC is any client application that requests a computation from a PCE. The RFC makes no assumption about how a PCE is implemented and says the PCE function is orthogonal to a node's forwarding capability.

The RFC separates single PCE path computation (one PCE per domain per path) from multiple PCE path computation, and the centralized model (one PCE computes all paths in a domain) from the distributed model (the work is shared among PCEs). PCE can be used alongside other path computation models and is meant to match the Internet model of distributed functionality, not replace it.
sections.plainLanguage: A PCE is a helper that knows the map and finds a good route. A PCC is whoever asks it. Helpers can sit in your own machine or somewhere else.

sections.title: Why a PCE Is Needed
sections.content:
Section 4 gives examples where a separate PCE helps, and says the list is illustrative, not exhaustive.

  • CPU-intensive computation: placing a set of LSPs to optimize an objective, multi-criteria paths, or minimal cost point-to-multipoint trees may be too heavy for some routers.
  • Partial visibility: an ingress router cannot see inside another domain, so loose routes cannot guarantee an optimal or even viable path without trial and error.
  • No usable TED: keeping the Traffic Engineering Database can drain a node, or the IGP may lack TE extensions.
  • Outside the routing domain or no control plane: for example a customer-edge router, or legacy optical elements that only have data and management planes.
  • Backup paths and multi-layer networks: coordinated backup computation for bandwidth protection, and paths across client and server layers.
  • Path selection policy applied at the PCE.

The RFC also lists non-motivations. PCE is not meant for the whole Internet; it applies to a set of domains with known relationships, similar in scale to peering between Service Providers. A single centralized PCE also cannot guarantee that an LSP will be established.
sections.plainLanguage: A helper is useful when the map is too big for you, when you can only see your own country, or when your device is too small to do the math.

sections.title: The Basic PCE Configurations
sections.content:
Section 5 shows five ways to arrange PCEs.

  • Composite PCE node: a router that includes the PCE. The routing protocol feeds the TED, and the PCE operates on it, subject to local policy, to answer the node's own signaling engine.
  • External PCE: the head-end node sends a request to a separate PCE, which uses its own TED and returns a response.
  • Multiple PCE path computation: the returned path is partial or loose, so a downstream node consults another PCE for the next hops.
  • Multiple PCE with inter-PCE communication: the first PCE asks other PCEs for help. This is not a distributed computation algorithm, but it lets different PCEs compute different segments. The PCC may not see any difference from a centralized PCE.
  • Management-based use: a network management system acts as the PCC and gives the head-end LSR a fully computed explicit path.

The RFC lists the areas that need standardization: PCC-PCE and PCE-PCE communication, routing and signaling extensions for PCE discovery and inter-domain paths, metrics to evaluate path computation models, and MIB modules.
sections.plainLanguage: The helper can live inside your device, in a separate box, or you can have a chain of helpers passing the question along, one per country.

sections.title: Architectural Considerations
sections.content:
Section 6 covers the components and how they interact. PCE changes only how paths are computed, not how TE LSPs are signaled, maintained or torn down.

Discovery: a PCC must know where a PCE is, through configuration or a discovery mechanism, and requests are sent to a specific PCE, not broadcast. A PCC can pick among PCEs by their capabilities, such as supported constraints, computational capacity or whether they can compute point-to-multipoint trees. Liveness detection is called mandatory.

Communication: a request/response protocol carries the source and destination, bandwidth and QoS parameters, resources to use or avoid, the number of disjoint paths, and policy information. A failure returns an error with as much information as possible. The RFC makes no assumption that PCC-PCE and PCE-PCE protocols are identical.

TED synchronization can come from the IGP, from out-of-band retrieval, or from non-IGP sources such as operator-configured link usage policies and TE LSP data. A PCE may hold only a partial TED. A stateful PCE also tracks existing paths and reserved resources, which can improve results but needs reliable state synchronization; a stateless PCE treats each request independently.

Other topics are synchronized computation of several paths, confidentiality (a provider must not have to reveal its topology, so partial paths via loose hops must be possible), policy, unsolicited PCE updates, and crankback, where a failure is reported back to a domain boundary that tries another path.
sections.plainLanguage: You have to know which helper to ask, check that it is awake, and speak a language it understands. A helper that remembers every trip it has planned can plan better, but it has to keep a lot of notes.

sections.title: Evaluation and Manageability
sections.content:
Section 8 lists metrics for judging PCE-based solutions, not for choosing paths: optimality, scalability, load sharing, multi-path computation, reoptimization, path computation time, network stability, TED synchronization accuracy and speed, handling of unsatisfiable requests, and policy. It notes that improving one, such as path optimality, is likely to affect another, such as computation time.

Section 9 covers manageability. It must be possible to enable and disable the PCE function, with a graceful shutdown so a PCE does not just disappear. Operations are expected to be modeled with MIB modules, including statistics and notifications, with care not to flood the network with SNMP notifications. The architecture may increase TE LSP setup times and cause congestion if many requests arrive at once, so operators should be able to rate limit requests and a PCE should be able to report impending congestion.
sections.plainLanguage: You need a way to grade the helpers and a way to switch them on and off safely, without too many alarm bells.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A PCE-based architecture must be judged by its effect on the security of the routing and signaling already in the network. Intra-domain use is less likely to be an issue, but more inter-domain information flow and easier inter-domain path setup may increase vulnerability. Multi-domain solutions MUST examine their confidentiality effects.

Using a PCE that is not co-resident with the PCC adds specific risks: interception of requests or responses, impersonation of a PCE or PCC, falsification of TE information, policy information or PCE capabilities, and denial-of-service attacks on a PCE or its communication. The RFC expects PCE solutions to address these with authentication and security techniques, and expects applicability statements to carry detailed security sections.
sections.plainLanguage: If a stranger could pretend to be your trip planner, or read your questions, you would be in trouble. So the helpers must prove who they are.
